newsitem.title: USA: Northwest hydroelectric outlook seen normal so far.
newsitem.headline: Northwest hydroelectric outlook seen normal so far.

text.p: The outlook for Northwest hydroelectric generation during the upcoming water year is still uncertain, but industry sources say it is starting from a strong position and looks normal so far.
"For the year as a whole, it's been much wetter than normal," said a manager at Grant County Public Utility District in Washington state. "This spring was in the top three out of the last 50 years."
He also noted that recent fresh snowfall in the Cascade mountains was a good start for the current water year, typically calculated from October 1 through September 30.

According to the National Weather Service, precipitation in the Northwest was 118 percent of normal between October 1995 and September 1996. But rainfall during June through September was well-below normal.

The Bonneville Power Administration (BPA), which markets power produced at federal hydroelectric dams in the Northwest, is tentatively expecting a normal to somewhat-above-normal water year, said Nancy Stephen, head of BPA's weather and streamflow forecasting.
Although the agency's first official forecast will not be available until mid-December, several indicators point toward "a half-way decent year," she said.
These include "La Nina" weather patterns similar to those seen last year. La Nina's cooler equatorial ocean flows are the opposite of El Nino's warm flows.
In addition, the latest hurricane season, which is indirectly connected to La Nina, was more active than usual, another positive signal for precipitation volumes, Stephen said.
BPA even cites wider-than-normal stripes on a certain type of caterpillar as presaging a longer, wetter than normal winter.
The historical average for runoff at The Dalles, a key dam on the Columbia River, is 103 million acre feet. A normal water year could see anywhere between 90 and 110 million acre feet, noted Stephen.
Between January and July of this year, runoff at The Dalles totalled 139 million acre feet or 132 percent of normal levels.

According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, hydropower generation in Washington state was up 33 percent in January-July compared with the same 1995 period. Oregon's hydroelectric output was up 16 percent over the same period.
"Last year was an anomaly," said a trade source at Bonneville. "This year we haven't had record rainfall since June. At this point last year we had record rainfall every month since June."
He stressed that it was too early to tell what kind of water year was coming and the agency needed to go forward under the assumption that precipitation could be below normal.
Recent rain levels appear to be following a normal pattern, but in the end "any of 60 years of flow could occur," the BPA source said.
